name: Hydrogen
tagline: The simplest atom, and the most abundant in the universe
about: Hydrogen has a single proton and a single electron, making it the lightest element and the most common one in the universe. On Earth it is rarely found free; almost all of it is locked into water and organic compounds. As a pure substance it exists as H₂, a colorless gas that burns readily in air.
memoryHook: Hydrogen means water-former, from Greek hydro (water) and genes (forming) — it makes water when it burns.

name: Helium
tagline: Found in sunlight before it was found on Earth
about: Helium has a filled first shell, so it forms no ordinary compounds and exists as separate atoms rather than molecules. It has the lowest boiling point of any element and will not solidify at ordinary pressure, however far it is cooled. Most commercial helium is extracted from natural gas deposits.
memoryHook: Helium is named after Helios, the Greek sun god, because its spectral line was spotted in the Sun first.

name: Lithium
tagline: The lightest of all metals, and the one that powers phones
about: Lithium is a soft silvery metal light enough to float on water, which it reacts with steadily. Its single outer electron is given up easily, and that is exactly what makes it valuable in rechargeable batteries. Commercial supplies come from salt brines and from the mineral spodumene.
memoryHook: Lithium comes from Greek lithos, stone, because it was first identified in a mineral rather than in plant ash.

name: Beryllium
tagline: Stiff, light and nearly transparent to X-rays
about: Beryllium is a light metal that is unusually rigid for its mass, giving it a very high stiffness-to-weight ratio. It is also remarkably transparent to X-rays, so thin foils of it serve as windows in X-ray tubes and detectors. Most beryllium goes into copper alloys, where a small addition yields springs and contacts that resist fatigue.
memoryHook: Beryllium is named for beryl, the mineral that also gives us emerald and aquamarine.

name: Boron
discoveredBy: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, Louis Jacques Thenard and Humphry Davy
tagline: A metalloid that toughens glass and absorbs neutrons
about: Boron sits on the border between metals and non-metals, and in pure form it is a hard, dark, brittle solid built from linked icosahedral clusters. Added to glass as borate, it makes cookware and laboratory ware resistant to thermal shock. Boron-10 is a strong neutron absorber, which is why it is used in reactor control rods.
memoryHook: Boron takes its name from borax, the mineral it was first extracted from, plus an ending borrowed from carbon.
elementalForm: B — covalent network of B₁₂ units

name: Carbon
tagline: The backbone of every molecule life is built from
about: Carbon forms four strong bonds and links readily to itself, which allows an enormous variety of chains, rings and sheets. That versatility underpins all known organic chemistry and every living organism. As a pure element it appears as graphite, as diamond, and in engineered forms such as nanotubes and graphene.
memoryHook: Carbon comes from Latin carbo, charcoal — the black residue people burned long before the element was named.

name: Nitrogen
tagline: Four-fifths of the air, and famously unreactive
about: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the atmosphere as N₂, held together by a triple bond that is very hard to break. That inertness is why it is used to blanket reactive materials, and why converting it into fertiliser takes so much energy. Nitrogen atoms appear in every amino acid and in DNA.
memoryHook: Nitrogen means nitre-forming, after saltpetre (potassium nitrate), the mineral it was first linked to.

name: Oxygen
discoveredBy: Carl Wilhelm Scheele and Joseph Priestley
tagline: The element that makes fire and breathing possible
about: Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust and the third most abundant in the universe. As O₂ it supports respiration and combustion, both of which release energy by forming bonds to oxygen. Nearly all the free oxygen in the atmosphere was produced by photosynthesis over billions of years.
memoryHook: Oxygen means acid-former, from Greek oxys, sharp — an early and mistaken idea that all acids contained it.

name: Fluorine
tagline: The most electronegative element there is
about: Fluorine is a pale yellow gas that reacts with almost every other element, often violently. Isolating it defeated chemists for decades until Moissan succeeded using low-temperature electrolysis. Once bonded, however, fluorine forms some of the most stable compounds known, including PTFE and many refrigerants.
memoryHook: Fluorine is named from Latin fluere, to flow, because fluorite was used as a flux to make ores melt more easily.

name: Neon
tagline: A quiet gas that glows an unmistakable orange-red
about: Neon has a full outer shell, so it exists as single unbonded atoms and forms no stable compounds. Passing an electric discharge through low-pressure neon excites its electrons, which emit a distinctive orange-red light as they drop back down. It is obtained in small quantities by distilling liquefied air.
memoryHook: Neon is Greek for new — Ramsay's son suggested the name when the gas turned up as a newly found part of air.

name: Sodium
tagline: The metal hiding in every grain of table salt
about: Sodium is a soft silvery metal that reacts vigorously with water, so it is never found uncombined in nature. It occurs instead in compounds such as sodium chloride, the salt dissolved in seawater. Its single outer electron is given up easily, forming the Na⁺ ion that every living cell depends on.
memoryHook: Na comes from the Latin natrium, from natron, the soda mineral Egyptians used for preserving and cleaning.

name: Magnesium
discoveredBy: Joseph Black; first isolated by Humphry Davy in 1808
tagline: Light enough to fly, bright enough to burn
about: Magnesium is a light structural metal, roughly two-thirds the density of aluminum, and its alloys turn up in car parts, aircraft and laptop shells. Once ignited it burns with an intense white flame. In plants, a single magnesium ion sits at the center of every chlorophyll molecule.
memoryHook: Named after Magnesia, a district in Greece that also lent its name to manganese and to the magnet.

name: Aluminum
tagline: Once costlier than gold, now everywhere
about: Aluminum is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust, yet it is bound so tightly into minerals that it was long a laboratory curiosity. The Hall-Héroult process of 1886 made electrical extraction cheap enough for mass production. A thin oxide film forms instantly on the surface and shields the metal from corrosion.
memoryHook: The name traces back to alum, the astringent salt known since antiquity, which is why the symbol is Al.

name: Silicon
tagline: Sand refined into the logic of computers
about: Silicon is a hard, brittle metalloid that makes up about a quarter of the Earth's crust, mostly as quartz and silicate minerals. Ultrapure single crystals of it form the base material for transistors and solar cells. Adding traces of other elements tunes its semiconducting behavior with great precision.
memoryHook: Silicon comes from Latin silex, meaning flint. Silicon is the element; silicone is the rubbery polymer made from it.

name: Phosphorus
tagline: Glows in the dark, feeds the world's crops
about: Phosphorus comes in several forms: white phosphorus is built from P₄ molecules and ignites in air, while red phosphorus is far more stable. Hennig Brand obtained it in 1669 by boiling down urine, making it the first element with a named discoverer. Phosphate groups form the backbone of DNA.
memoryHook: From the Greek phosphoros, light-bearer, for the faint glow white phosphorus gives off as it reacts with air.

name: Sulfur
tagline: Brimstone yellow, and industry's workhorse
about: Sulfur is a brittle yellow solid built from crown-shaped S₈ rings, found near volcanic vents and in vast underground deposits. Most of it is converted into sulfuric acid, the most heavily produced industrial chemical in the world. Two amino acids contain sulfur, and the bridges they form help hold proteins in shape.
memoryHook: Brimstone, sulfur's older name, is Old English for burning stone. Let the symbol S stand for the S₈ crown ring.

name: Chlorine
tagline: A green gas that keeps drinking water clean
about: Chlorine is a dense yellow-green gas with a sharp odor and a powerful pull on electrons from other atoms. Industry makes it by passing electricity through brine. Joined with sodium it becomes ordinary table salt, and its compounds are widely used to disinfect water supplies and to make plastics.
memoryHook: From the Greek chloros, pale green, which is exactly the color of the gas when you see a flask of it.

name: Argon
tagline: Abundant, unreactive and quietly useful
about: Argon makes up just under one percent of the atmosphere, more than any other noble gas, and is separated on a huge scale from liquid air. Its filled outer shell leaves it almost completely unreactive. That inertness makes it a protective blanket for welding and a filling for lamps and double-glazed windows.
memoryHook: From the Greek argos, idle or lazy, a name chosen because the gas refused to react with anything offered to it.

name: Potassium
tagline: The spark behind every nerve signal
about: Potassium is a soft alkali metal stored under oil because it reacts violently with moisture, releasing hydrogen that often ignites. Davy isolated it in 1807 by electrolyzing molten potash, the first metal ever obtained that way. Potassium ions crossing cell membranes carry the signals of nerve and muscle.
memoryHook: K is for kalium, from the Arabic al-qalyah, plant ashes; the English name comes from potash, ash from a pot.

name: Calcium
tagline: Structure for bone, stone and cement
about: Calcium is a reactive silvery metal, though most people meet it through its compounds: limestone, chalk, marble and gypsum. Heating limestone drives off carbon dioxide to give quicklime, a key step in making cement. In vertebrates, crystals of calcium phosphate give bone and teeth their hardness.
memoryHook: From the Latin calx, meaning lime, the burnt limestone Roman builders mixed into mortar and the root of the word chalk.

name: Scandium
tagline: Light, thinly spread, and transformative in aluminum
about: Scandium is a light transition metal that Mendeleev predicted before anyone found it. It is spread thinly through the crust rather than concentrated in rich ores, so it is costly to obtain. Small additions to aluminum give exceptionally strong, weldable alloys used in aerospace and sports equipment.
memoryHook: Scandium is named for Scandia, the Latin name for Scandinavia, where Nilson first separated it from Nordic ores.

name: Titanium
tagline: Strong as steel, light enough to fly
about: Titanium matches the strength of many steels at roughly half the weight, and a thin oxide film makes it highly resistant to corrosion. Separating it from its ores is difficult, which keeps the metal expensive. Most titanium mined is used as titanium dioxide, a brilliant white pigment.
memoryHook: Klaproth named it for the Titans of Greek myth — titanic strength in a metal light enough to build aircraft from.

name: Vanadium
tagline: Named for a goddess, prized for its toughness
about: Vanadium is a hard, silvery metal whose compounds show striking colors across several oxidation states. Almost all of it goes into steel, where even a small fraction produces tough, shock-resistant alloys for tools and springs. Vanadium pentoxide also catalyses sulfuric acid production.
memoryHook: Named for Vanadís, a byname of the Norse goddess Freyja, chosen for the beauty of its colored compounds.

name: Chromium
tagline: Hard, bright, and named for color
about: Chromium takes a mirror finish and forms a thin, self-repairing oxide film that shields the metal beneath, which is why stainless steel resists rust. Its name reflects the vivid colors of its compounds, from chrome yellow to deep green. Traces of chromium in corundum are what make rubies red.
memoryHook: From the Greek chroma, meaning color — think chrome trim and the chromatic range of its compounds.

name: Manganese
tagline: The quiet partner in almost every steel
about: Manganese is a brittle metal rarely used pure, yet nearly all steel contains some because it strips sulfur and oxygen out during refining. Its dioxide sits at the heart of alkaline batteries, and permanganate salts are powerful oxidizing agents. It is also an essential trace element for plants and animals.
memoryHook: Manganese and magnesium both trace back to Magnesia in Greece; Mn is the heavier, harder member of the pair.

name: Iron
tagline: The metal that built civilisations
about: Iron is the most widely used metal on Earth and the backbone of steel. It also marks the point where fusion inside stars stops releasing energy, so iron builds up in stellar cores. In living things it sits at the center of hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen through the blood.
memoryHook: Fe comes from the Latin ferrum — the same root behind ferrous, ferrite and farrier.

name: Cobalt
tagline: Blue in glass, magnetic in metal
about: Cobalt has colored glass and ceramics a deep blue for centuries. Today most of it goes into lithium-ion battery cathodes and into superalloys that hold their strength inside jet engines. Much of the world's supply comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which makes sourcing a live issue.
memoryHook: Cobalt comes from kobold, the German goblin miners blamed for ore that looked like copper, smelled foul and yielded none.

name: Nickel
tagline: Corrosion-resistant workhorse of modern alloys
about: Nickel resists corrosion and keeps its strength at high temperature, which makes it central to stainless steel and to the superalloys used in turbine blades. It is also a major component of rechargeable battery cathodes. Earth's core is thought to be largely an iron-nickel alloy.
memoryHook: From Kupfernickel, or devil's copper — ore that looked like copper but stubbornly yielded none.

name: Copper
tagline: Ancient craft metal, modern electrical backbone
about: Copper conducts electricity better than any metal except silver and is ductile enough to be drawn into hair-thin wire. People have smelted and worked it for thousands of years: alloyed with tin it gives bronze, and with zinc, brass. Exposed to damp air it slowly grows a green patina of copper carbonate and sulfate salts.
memoryHook: Cu comes from cuprum, shortened from aes Cyprium, 'metal of Cyprus' — the island whose mines supplied Rome.

name: Zinc
tagline: The sacrificial shield that keeps steel intact
about: Zinc is used mainly to galvanize steel: the coating corrodes in place of the iron beneath, protecting it even where the surface is scratched. Alloyed with copper it becomes brass, and it drives zinc-carbon and zinc-air cells. Zinc ions also sit at the active site of many enzymes.
memoryHook: Zinc likely comes from the German Zinke, meaning prong, for the tooth-like crystals left in the smelting furnace.

name: Gallium
tagline: A metal that melts in the warmth of a hand
about: Gallium is a soft silvery metal with a melting point just above room temperature, so a solid piece turns liquid when held. It is rarely found alone in nature and is recovered mainly from bauxite and zinc ores. Its compounds drive LEDs, laser diodes and high-frequency chips.
memoryHook: Named for Gallia, the Latin name for France, homeland of its discoverer Lecoq de Boisbaudran.

name: Germanium
tagline: The metalloid that launched the transistor age
about: Germanium is a brittle gray-white metalloid that forms a diamond-like covalent network. The first transistors were built from it before silicon took over, and it remains important in infrared optics and fiber-optic glass. Mendeleev predicted its properties years before anyone found it.
memoryHook: Winkler named it for Germany, his homeland; Mendeleev had called the empty slot eka-silicon.

name: Arsenic
tagline: Infamous poison, quietly essential to electronics
about: Arsenic's stable gray form is a brittle metalloid built from puckered covalent layers, and it sublimes rather than melting at ordinary pressure. Its compounds are highly toxic and were long used as pigments and pesticides. Today gallium arsenide makes it valuable in fast semiconductors and laser diodes.
memoryHook: The symbol As comes from the Greek arsenikon; picture arsenic As the classic detective-story poison.

name: Selenium
discoveredBy: Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Johan Gottlieb Gahn
tagline: The element that made office copying possible
about: Selenium's gray form is built from long helical chains of atoms, and it conducts electricity far better in light than in darkness. That photoconductivity powered early photocopiers and light meters. Selenium is also an essential trace element, built into enzymes in many organisms.
memoryHook: Berzelius named it for Selene, Greek goddess of the Moon, to pair it with tellurium, named for Earth.

name: Bromine
tagline: The only nonmetal liquid at room temperature
about: Bromine is a dense red-brown liquid of Br₂ molecules that gives off a sharp, choking vapor. It is extracted from seawater and salt brines, where bromide ions are concentrated enough to harvest. Its compounds have served as flame retardants, photographic chemicals and agricultural fumigants.
memoryHook: From the Greek bromos, stench, for its sharp smell; picture Br as the brown liquid that reeks.

name: Krypton
tagline: A hidden gas that glows brilliant white in lamps
about: Krypton is a colorless noble gas present in trace amounts in air and obtained by distilling liquefied air. Its full outer shell makes it almost unreactive, though chemists have coaxed it into compounds such as krypton difluoride. In high-intensity lamps and camera flashes it gives an intense white light.
memoryHook: From the Greek kryptos, hidden, because Ramsay and Travers found it concealed in leftover liquid air.

name: Rubidium
tagline: A soft metal that keeps atomic clocks honest
about: Rubidium is a silvery alkali metal so soft and reactive that it tarnishes instantly in air and reacts violently with water. It was among the first elements found by spectroscopy, recognized from deep red lines in a flame. Rubidium atoms now supply the reference frequency in many atomic clocks.
memoryHook: Named from the Latin rubidus, deep red, for the two crimson spectral lines Bunsen and Kirchhoff saw.

name: Strontium
tagline: The crimson in fireworks and signal flares
about: Strontium is a reactive silvery alkaline earth metal that tarnishes quickly in air. Its salts color a flame brilliant scarlet, which is why they appear in fireworks and emergency flares. Because strontium behaves chemically much like calcium, the fallout isotope strontium-90 can settle in bone.
memoryHook: Named for Strontian, the Scottish village whose lead mine yielded the mineral strontianite.

name: Yttrium
tagline: The quiet metal behind color screens and lasers
about: Yttrium is a silvery transition metal that behaves much like the lanthanides and is mined alongside them. Its oxide hosts the phosphors that gave older color televisions their red, and yttrium aluminum garnet forms the crystal in YAG lasers. It also stabilises zirconia ceramics and superconducting oxides.
memoryHook: Yttrium, ytterbium, erbium and terbium all take their names from Ytterby, one small quarry in Sweden.

name: Zirconium
tagline: Corrosion-resistant armor for nuclear fuel
about: Zirconium is a strong, corrosion-resistant transition metal that barely absorbs neutrons, which makes its alloys the standard cladding for nuclear fuel. Its main ore, zircon, yields crystals that geologists date back billions of years. Cubic zirconia, a synthetic oxide, is a familiar diamond substitute.
memoryHook: From the mineral zircon, itself from the Persian zargun, gold-colored; Zr sits just below titanium.

name: Niobium
tagline: The superconductor inside an MRI scanner
about: Niobium is a soft, ductile transition metal protected by a thin, tough oxide layer. Alloyed with tin or titanium it becomes a superconductor, which is how it ends up in MRI scanners and particle accelerators. Small additions of niobium also make high-strength steels tougher without adding weight.
memoryHook: Named after Niobe, daughter of Tantalus — niobium sits directly above tantalum, the element named for her father.

name: Molybdenum
discoveredBy: Peter Jacob Hjelm (first isolation; identified by Carl Wilhelm Scheele in 1778)
tagline: Hardens steel and keeps machinery turning
about: Molybdenum has one of the highest melting points of any element, which suits it to furnace parts and high-temperature alloys. It also sits at the center of enzymes that let bacteria and plants handle nitrogen and sulfur. Its layered sulfide flakes apart under pressure, making a slippery solid lubricant.
memoryHook: From the Greek molybdos, meaning lead: its dark, soft ore was mistaken for lead ore for centuries.

name: Technetium
tagline: The first element made rather than found
about: Technetium was the first element obtained by artificial means, filling a stubborn gap in the periodic table. Every one of its isotopes is radioactive, so it is all but absent from Earth's crust apart from traces in uranium ores. Today it is produced in reactors and in small bench generators for imaging work.
memoryHook: Technetium comes from the Greek tekhnetos, artificial — the first element made by technology rather than dug out of the ground.

name: Ruthenium
tagline: A platinum cousin hidden in hard drives
about: Ruthenium is a hard, brittle member of the platinum group, recovered mainly as a by-product of nickel and platinum refining. Thin ruthenium layers help pack data more densely onto hard-disk platters. Its compounds are prized catalysts, from ammonia synthesis to the metathesis reactions used in organic chemistry.
memoryHook: Named after Ruthenia, the Latin name for Rus: Claus isolated it at Kazan, so read Ru as the Russian platinum metal.

name: Rhodium
tagline: Rarer than gold, and it cleans exhaust
about: Rhodium is one of the rarest metals in Earth's crust, and its price often runs well above gold's. Most of it goes into catalytic converters, where it turns nitrogen oxides from engine exhaust back into nitrogen and oxygen. Its bright, tarnish-free surface is also the usual plating on white gold jewelry.
memoryHook: From the Greek rhodon, rose: Wollaston named it for the rose-red color of its salt solutions.

name: Palladium
tagline: The metal that drinks hydrogen
about: Palladium can absorb many times its own volume of hydrogen, and it lets that gas diffuse through the metal while blocking others. The same surface chemistry makes it a superb catalyst, used in vehicle exhaust systems and in the carbon-carbon coupling reactions that build complex organic molecules.
memoryHook: Named after Pallas, the asteroid found only months earlier — Wollaston borrowed a brand-new name from the sky for a brand-new metal.

name: Silver
tagline: No element conducts electricity better
about: Silver has the highest electrical and thermal conductivity of any element, which is why it turns up in switch contacts, conductive pastes and solar-cell grids. Worked since antiquity into coins and tableware, it does not rust; the familiar black tarnish comes from reacting with sulfur compounds in the air.
memoryHook: Ag stands for the Latin argentum. Argentina was named for silver too, so the country name doubles as a reminder.

name: Cadmium
discoveredBy: Friedrich Stromeyer (independently by Karl Samuel Leberecht Hermann)
tagline: Painter's yellow, now largely regulated away
about: Cadmium is a soft, silvery metal with a low melting point, long used for protective plating and in rechargeable nickel-cadmium cells. Its compounds give artists the intense cadmium yellow, orange and red pigments. Because the metal is toxic and accumulates in tissue, many of those uses are now restricted.
memoryHook: From cadmia, the old name for zinc ore: cadmium was found hiding as an impurity in zinc, and it still sits just below zinc in the table.

name: Indium
discoveredBy: Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymous Theodor Richter
tagline: Named for indigo, working under the screen
about: Indium is a silvery metal soft enough to mark with a fingernail, and it melts at a lower temperature than most metals. Combined with tin and oxygen it forms indium tin oxide, a coating that is transparent yet conducting, which is what lets a touchscreen sense a finger. Most indium comes from zinc-refining residues.
memoryHook: Named for the indigo-blue line it threw in the spectroscope — In for indigo, the color that gave the new element away.

name: Tin
tagline: Half of bronze, and the age it made possible
about: Tin is a soft, low-melting metal that has been alloyed with copper to make bronze for thousands of years. Held cold for long stretches, shiny white tin slowly crumbles into a gray powder known as tin pest. Most tin today goes into solder and into the thin coating that protects steel food cans.
memoryHook: Sn comes from the Latin stannum, the Roman word for tin — the same root behind chemical terms like stannous and stannic.

name: Antimony
tagline: The metalloid that slows a fire down
about: Antimony is a brittle, silvery metalloid worked since antiquity and won mainly from the mineral stibnite. It rarely appears alone in modern products; instead it hardens lead alloys, and as antimony trioxide it helps plastics and textiles resist catching fire.
memoryHook: Sb comes from the Latin stibium, the name for stibnite, the ore ground into black eye paint in the ancient world.

name: Tellurium
tagline: Named for the Earth, useful in sunlight
about: Tellurium is a scarce, brittle metalloid whose atoms link into long spiral chains in the solid. It is recovered mainly as a by-product of copper refining. Most of it ends up in cadmium telluride solar panels and in bismuth telluride devices that move heat when current flows through them.
memoryHook: Tellurium takes its name from the Latin tellus, meaning earth, while its neighbor selenium was named for the moon.

name: Iodine
tagline: Violet vapor with a serious job
about: Iodine is the heaviest halogen found in quantity on Earth, and exists as I₂ molecules stacked into dark, glossy crystals. Warmed gently, it sublimes straight to a violet vapor. The thyroid needs trace amounts to build its hormones, which is why much of the world's table salt is iodised.
memoryHook: The name comes from the Greek iodes, meaning violet, the color of the vapor Courtois saw rising from seaweed ash.

name: Xenon
tagline: A stranger gas that lights the road
about: Xenon is a dense, colorless noble gas present in tiny traces in the atmosphere. Its outer shell is full, so it reacts only under forcing conditions, yet chemists have made genuine compounds such as xenon tetrafluoride. Electrically excited, it glows with a blue-white light.
memoryHook: Ramsay named it from the Greek xenos, meaning stranger, because it was the odd new gas left over after argon and krypton.

name: Cesium
tagline: Soft, golden, and keeper of the second
about: Cesium is a soft, gold-tinged alkali metal that melts barely above room temperature and reacts vigorously with water. Its single outer electron is held so loosely that ordinary light can knock it free. A precise microwave transition in cesium-133 defines the length of the SI second.
memoryHook: Bunsen named it from the Latin caesius, sky blue, after the two blue lines it showed in his spectroscope.

name: Barium
tagline: Heavy by name, green by firelight
about: Barium is a soft, reactive alkaline earth metal that tarnishes within seconds in air and is never found uncombined in nature. Its salts color flames a deep green. Barium sulfate is a striking exception: so insoluble that it passes through the gut unchanged, and dense enough to cast a clear X-ray shadow.
memoryHook: The name comes from the Greek barys, meaning heavy, after the unusually dense mineral barite it was first found in.

name: Lanthanum
tagline: The hidden one that named a series
about: Lanthanum opens the lanthanide series, yet its own configuration skips the 4f subshell and places the extra electron in 5d instead. The soft metal tarnishes rapidly in air. It turns up in nickel-metal hydride battery electrodes and in optical glass with a high refractive index.
memoryHook: From the Greek lanthanein, to lie hidden: it stayed concealed inside cerium minerals until Mosander teased it out.

name: Cerium
discoveredBy: Jöns Jacob Berzelius and Wilhelm Hisinger
tagline: The rare earth that is not rare
about: Cerium is the most abundant of the rare earth elements, more common in the crust than tin. It moves easily between the +3 and +4 oxidation states, which lets cerium oxide absorb and release oxygen inside catalytic converters. Alloyed with iron, it forms the sparking flint in lighters.
memoryHook: Cerium was named after the asteroid Ceres, spotted just two years before the element was identified.

name: Praseodymium
tagline: The green twin of the didymium pair
about: Praseodymium appeared in 1885 when Carl Auer von Welsbach split didymium, long assumed to be a single element, into two. Its compounds are green, and the metal stiffens neodymium magnets and the magnesium alloys used in aircraft engines. Glass containing it filters the yellow glare of hot metalwork.
memoryHook: From the Greek prasios didymos, green twin, for the color of its salts and its origin inside didymium.

name: Neodymium
tagline: Small magnets, outsized pull
about: Neodymium is a silvery lanthanide that oxidises quickly in air. Alloyed with iron and boron, it forms the strongest permanent magnets in commercial use, which is why it turns up in headphone drivers, hard drives and wind turbine generators. Its glass looks lavender by day and shifts blue under fluorescent light.
memoryHook: From the Greek neos didymos, new twin: Welsbach pulled it out of didymium alongside praseodymium in the same work.

name: Promethium
discoveredBy: Jacob A. Marinsky, Lawrence E. Glendenin and Charles D. Coryell
tagline: The lanthanide with no stable isotope
about: Promethium is the only lanthanide with no stable isotope, so it is essentially absent from Earth's crust and is produced in nuclear reactors. Its most studied isotope, promethium-147, has a half-life of about 2.6 years and emits beta particles. Promethium salts glow faintly as a result of that radiation.
memoryHook: Named for Prometheus, who stole fire for humanity - a fitting name for a glowing element that had to be created rather than found.

name: Samarium
tagline: Magnets that keep their nerve when hot
about: Samarium is a silvery lanthanide best known in samarium-cobalt magnets, which hold their magnetism at temperatures that weaken most other rare-earth magnets. It was the first element named after a person, by way of the mineral samarskite. The isotope samarium-149 also absorbs neutrons strongly inside reactors.
memoryHook: Samarium comes from samarskite, named for the mining official Vasili Samarsky-Bykhovets - the first element named after a person.

name: Europium
tagline: The glow behind red on a screen
about: Europium is the most reactive lanthanide, tarnishing almost immediately in air and reacting with water. Its ions are exceptional phosphors: europium(III) emits red light and europium(II) emits blue. That property carried it from color television tubes into modern LED lighting and the security inks printed on banknotes.
memoryHook: Europium is named after Europe, which pairs neatly with americium, the element named for the Americas.

name: Gadolinium
tagline: A metal that warms when magnetized
about: Gadolinium carries seven unpaired 4f electrons, which gives it the largest thermal neutron capture cross-section of any stable element and striking magnetic behavior. It loses its ferromagnetism just below room temperature and warms measurably in a magnetic field, the magnetocaloric effect behind experimental cooling systems.
memoryHook: Named for Johan Gadolin, who studied the Ytterby minerals; Gd breaks the pattern with a half-filled 4f shell plus one 5d electron.

name: Terbium
tagline: Green light and metal that changes shape
about: Terbium is a soft silvery lanthanide whose compounds emit a strong green glow, making it a standard phosphor in lamps and displays. Alloyed with dysprosium and iron it forms Terfenol-D, a material that stretches noticeably in a magnetic field and drives sonar transducers and precision actuators.
memoryHook: Terbium, erbium, ytterbium and yttrium are all named after one Swedish quarry, Ytterby; terbium takes the letters t-e-r-b.

name: Dysprosium
tagline: Keeps powerful magnets working under heat
about: Dysprosium is added in small amounts to neodymium-iron-boron magnets so they resist demagnetising when hot, which matters in electric-vehicle motors and wind turbines. It has one of the largest magnetic moments of any element and also appears in magnetostrictive alloys and neutron-absorbing control rods.
memoryHook: From the Greek dysprositos, hard to get at - it resisted separation through dozens of attempts before it was isolated.

name: Holmium
tagline: The highest magnetic moment in nature
about: Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any naturally occurring element, so it is shaped into pole pieces that concentrate the field of the strongest laboratory magnets. Its sharp, stable absorption lines also make holmium oxide glass a standard reference for calibrating spectrophotometers.
memoryHook: Holmium is named after Holmia, the Latin name for Stockholm - another Swedish entry in the crowded rare-earth row.

name: Erbium
tagline: The element that keeps the internet lit
about: Erbium ions embedded in silica fiber amplify light near 1550 nanometers, the wavelength that travels furthest through glass. Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers boost signals along undersea cables without converting them back into electricity. Erbium compounds also tint glass and ceramic glazes a soft pink.
memoryHook: Carl Gustaf Mosander pulled erbium and terbium from the same Ytterby ore, naming each for a different slice of the village name.

name: Thulium
tagline: Rarest of the stable lanthanides
about: Thulium is the least abundant lanthanide that has a stable isotope, which long kept it costly and little used. The isotope thulium-170 emits X-rays and powers small portable radiography sources, while thulium-doped crystals produce infrared laser light near two micrometers.
memoryHook: Thulium is named after Thule, the far-northern land of ancient geography - a remote name for the rarest stable lanthanide.

name: Ytterbium
tagline: At the heart of optical lattice clocks
about: Ytterbium is a soft silvery metal with a filled 4f shell, so its chemistry resembles calcium more than that of its lanthanide neighbours. Trapped ytterbium atoms and ions underpin optical lattice clocks, among the most precise timekeepers ever built, and ytterbium-doped fibers make powerful industrial lasers.
memoryHook: Ytterby in Sweden lent its name to four elements; ytterbium keeps most of the village name and sits at number 70.

name: Lutetium
discoveredBy: Georges Urbain and Carl Auer von Welsbach
tagline: Rare, costly, and last of the lanthanides
about: Lutetium closes the lanthanide series and is among the rarest and most costly rare-earth metals to purify. Its oxide serves as a catalyst in petroleum refining, and the slow decay of lutetium-176 lets geologists date meteorites and ancient crustal rocks. Lutetium oxyorthosilicate crystals also give PET scanners their fast, bright detectors.
memoryHook: Named for Lutetia, the Roman name for Paris, where Georges Urbain separated it in 1907.

name: Hafnium
discoveredBy: Dirk Coster and George de Hevesy
tagline: A neutron sponge at the heart of reactors
about: Hafnium sits directly below zirconium and clings to it so closely in ores that the two were not separated until 1923. It absorbs neutrons far more strongly than zirconium, so it is shaped into reactor control rods, and its carbide melts higher than almost any known compound.
memoryHook: Hafnia is the Latin name for Copenhagen, where Coster and de Hevesy identified it at Bohr's institute.

name: Tantalum
tagline: Quietly holding the charge inside your phone
about: Tantalum is dense, strongly corrosion resistant, and grows a thin oxide film that behaves as an excellent insulator. That film makes it the core of the compact capacitors packed into phones and laptops. Most tantalum comes from coltan ore, which has raised long-running concerns about conflict sourcing.
memoryHook: Named for Tantalus, who stood in water he could never drink; the metal likewise refuses to take up acid.

name: Tungsten
tagline: The metal that refuses to melt
about: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, which is why it glowed as the filament in incandescent bulbs for the better part of a century. Bonded with carbon it forms tungsten carbide, hard enough to cut and drill hardened steel. It is also remarkably dense for its cost.
memoryHook: The symbol W comes from wolfram, from a German phrase about ore that devoured tin the way a wolf takes sheep.

name: Rhenium
discoveredBy: Walter Noddack, Ida Tacke and Otto Berg
tagline: The final stable element to be discovered
about: Rhenium was the final element with a stable isotope to be discovered, in 1925, and it stays one of the scarcest metals in Earth's crust. Its melting point is second only to tungsten, so it strengthens the single-crystal turbine blades of jet engines. Refineries rely on rhenium catalysts to raise petrol octane.
memoryHook: Named after the Rhine, Rhenus in Latin, the home river of its three German discoverers.

name: Osmium
tagline: The densest element found in nature
about: Osmium is the densest naturally occurring element, edging out iridium, so a small block feels startlingly heavy. It is hard and brittle, and it turns up in platinum ores as a by-product of refining. Its powder reacts with air to form a volatile oxide with a sharp, penetrating smell.
memoryHook: From the Greek osme, meaning smell, after the pungent odor of osmium tetroxide.

name: Iridium
tagline: Acids leave this metal alone
about: Iridium is the most corrosion-resistant metal known, untouched by acids even when hot. A thin iridium-rich clay layer found worldwide marks the end of the Cretaceous and supports the case for a large asteroid impact. Today it tips spark plugs and lines crucibles for growing crystals.
memoryHook: Named for Iris, the Greek goddess of the rainbow, because iridium salts take on many colors.

name: Platinum
tagline: The catalyst cleaning the air behind you
about: Platinum is valued both as a jewelry metal and as a catalyst, since its surface lets gas molecules react with each other without being used up. Catalytic converters rely on it alongside palladium and rhodium to scrub exhaust gases. Its configuration is anomalous: one 6s electron shifts into the 5d shell.
memoryHook: From the Spanish platina, little silver, the dismissive name colonial miners gave it as an unwanted impurity in gold.

name: Gold
tagline: Never tarnishes, never out of fashion
about: Gold is soft, extraordinarily malleable, and one of the few metals that does not tarnish in air, which is why buried artifacts still gleam after thousands of years. It conducts electricity well, so a thin plating protects critical connectors. Almost all the gold ever mined still exists above ground, recycled again and again.
memoryHook: Au comes from the Latin aurum, shining dawn, while the English word gold traces to a root meaning yellow.

name: Mercury
tagline: The only metal that pours at room temperature
about: Mercury is the one metal that is liquid at room temperature, because its tightly held outer electrons bond only weakly between atoms. It once filled thermometers and barometers, but its toxicity and environmental persistence have driven those uses out under the Minamata Convention. Its vapor glows when energised, which still lights fluorescent tubes.
memoryHook: Hg is short for hydrargyrum, Greek for water-silver; the English name comes from Mercury, the swift Roman messenger god.

name: Thallium
tagline: Soft, silvery, and quietly infamous
about: Thallium is a soft, silvery metal that tarnishes within minutes in air. Its salts are colorless, odorless and tasteless, which made them a common rodent and insect killer and, notoriously, a poisoner's tool. Most thallium now goes into infrared optical glass and electronic detectors.
memoryHook: Greek thallos, a green shoot: Crookes named it for the bright green line he saw in its spectrum.

name: Lead
tagline: Heavy, ancient, and hard to leave behind
about: Lead is a dense, soft metal that people have smelted for thousands of years because it melts easily and resists corrosion. Those same qualities made it common in pipes, paint and fuel long before its toxicity was understood. Most lead handled today, new or recycled, ends up in lead-acid batteries.
memoryHook: Pb comes from Latin plumbum, the same root as plumber and plumb line, both trades lead once defined.

name: Bismuth
tagline: The gentle giant at the edge of stability
about: Bismuth is a brittle metal with a faint pink cast that grows stair-stepped hopper crystals when it cools slowly. Bismuth-209 was listed for decades as the heaviest stable nuclide, until its alpha decay was finally measured in 2003. Its low toxicity makes it a common stand-in for lead.
memoryHook: From German Wismut, usually read as weisse Masse, white mass; Bi keeps bismuth's first two letters.

name: Polonium
tagline: Curie's first find, named for a vanished country
about: Polonium was the first element Marie and Pierre Curie separated from uranium ore, and they named it for Poland. It is fiercely radioactive: half a gram heats itself to several hundred degrees, and the ionized air around it glows blue. Sealed sources have been used to bleed static off machinery.
memoryHook: Po for Poland. Marie Curie named it for her homeland, which had been erased from the map of Europe.

name: Astatine
discoveredBy: Dale Corson, Kenneth MacKenzie and Emilio Segrè
tagline: Rarer than anything else the Earth makes
about: Astatine is the rarest naturally occurring element, with well under a gram spread through the entire crust at any moment. Every isotope decays within hours, so no weighable sample has ever been seen, and most listed properties are extrapolated from iodine and bromine. Work now centers on astatine-211.
memoryHook: Greek astatos, unstable, is the name and the warning; At sits under iodine as the halogen that vanishes.

name: Radon
tagline: A noble gas that drifts up out of the ground
about: Radon is a dense, colorless noble gas released as uranium and thorium decay inside rock and soil. Because it is chemically inert, it seeps through foundations and collects in basements, where inexpensive detectors track it. Its commonest isotope, radon-222, has a half-life of just under four days.
memoryHook: Radon is radium's breath: it was first called radium emanation, and Rn still carries the parent's name.

name: Francium
tagline: The alkali metal that never sits still
about: Francium is the least stable of the alkali metals, and its longest-lived isotope lasts about twenty-two minutes. No more than a few hundred thousand atoms have been gathered at once, held in laser and magnetic traps. Almost everything known about it comes from spectroscopy rather than bench chemistry.
memoryHook: Marguerite Perey named it for France. Francium was the last element found in nature rather than made.

name: Radium
tagline: The element that made the dark hands glow
about: Radium is a silvery alkaline earth metal whose radiation excites nearby air into a faint glow. Marie and Pierre Curie separated it from tonnes of pitchblende residue in 1898, and it briefly became a luxury ingredient. Before the hazards were understood it was painted onto watch dials and sold in tonics.
memoryHook: From Latin radius, a ray. Radium radiates, and the same root gives us radiation, radius and radio.

name: Actinium
tagline: The blue-glowing head of the actinide row
about: Actinium gives the actinide series its name and sits at the head of it. Freshly separated samples shine pale blue as their radiation ionizes the surrounding air. The metal is scarce, made mainly by irradiating radium with neutrons, and most current work involves its alpha emitter actinium-225.
memoryHook: Greek aktis, a ray or beam. Actinium leads the actinides, so Ac marks where the bottom row begins.

name: Thorium
tagline: Named for a thunder god, watched as a fuel
about: Thorium is a weakly radioactive metal about as abundant in the crust as lead. Its single primordial isotope, thorium-232, has a half-life close to the age of the universe, which is why it can still be mined. Absorbing a neutron turns it into uranium-233, the reason reactor designers keep returning to it.
memoryHook: Named for Thor, the Norse thunder god, by Berzelius; Thursday, Thor's day, carries the same name.

name: Protactinium
discoveredBy: Kasimir Fajans and Oswald Helmuth Göhring
tagline: Parent of actinium, scarce even in uranium ore
about: Protactinium is a dense, silvery actinide found in uranium ores in vanishingly small amounts; obtaining a few grams once meant processing tonnes of residue. Its name means parent of actinium, because protactinium-231 decays into actinium-227. Intensely radioactive, it remains a laboratory material with no bulk industrial role.
memoryHook: Proto- plus actinium: protactinium-231 decays into actinium-227, so it is literally the parent of actinium.

name: Uranium
tagline: Heavy, radioactive, fuel of the atomic age
about: Uranium is the heaviest element that occurs in the Earth's crust in substantial quantities. Natural uranium is mostly uranium-238 with about 0.7 percent uranium-235, the isotope that sustains a fission chain reaction. Enrichment raises that fraction for reactor fuel, while depleted uranium is used where extreme density is wanted.
memoryHook: Uranium was named after the planet Uranus, discovered eight years earlier; neptunium and plutonium then took the next two planet names.

name: Neptunium
tagline: The first element made beyond uranium
about: Neptunium was the first transuranium element to be created, made in 1940 by bombarding uranium with neutrons. It sits immediately past uranium in the table and took the name of the next planet outward. Trace amounts occur naturally in uranium ores, but nearly all neptunium on Earth is a by-product of reactors.
memoryHook: Neptune is the next planet name after Uranus, so neptunium (93) was named to follow uranium (92) in the table.

name: Plutonium
discoveredBy: Glenn T. Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy and Arthur Wahl
tagline: A manufactured metal that reshaped a century
about: Plutonium forms when uranium-238 absorbs a neutron and then undergoes two beta decays, so reactors produce it continuously. Plutonium-239 is fissile and central to nuclear weapons and mixed-oxide fuel, while plutonium-238 supplies steady heat for spacecraft power units. The metal is reactive and has six distinct solid forms.
memoryHook: Pluto follows Neptune, so Pu (94) follows Np (93); Seaborg picked the symbol Pu over the tidier Pl as a private joke.

name: Americium
discoveredBy: Glenn T. Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan and Albert Ghiorso
tagline: A synthetic actinide inside the smoke alarm
about: Americium is a synthetic actinide bred in reactors from plutonium. Americium-241 emits alpha particles at a very steady rate with a half-life of about 432 years, which makes it a convenient ionization source in household smoke detectors. The pure metal is silvery white and tarnishes slowly in air.
memoryHook: Americium sits directly below europium, and was named for the Americas exactly as europium was named for Europe.

name: Curium
discoveredBy: Glenn T. Seaborg, Ralph James and Albert Ghiorso
tagline: Named for the Curies, warmed by its own decay
about: Curium honours Marie and Pierre Curie and is made by bombarding plutonium with alpha particles. Its isotopes are radioactive enough that samples warm themselves and glow faintly purple. Curium has powered the alpha-particle X-ray spectrometers on Mars rovers, instruments that read the composition of rocks.
memoryHook: Curium sits under gadolinium, which honours the chemist Johan Gadolin; Cm honours Marie and Pierre Curie in the same way.

name: Berkelium
discoveredBy: Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso and Glenn T. Seaborg
tagline: Born in Berkeley, weighed in micrograms
about: Berkelium is a synthetic actinide first made in 1949 by bombarding americium with alpha particles in a cyclotron, and it is named for Berkeley, California, where that work was done. Only minute quantities have ever been separated, and its main role has been as a target for building heavier elements such as tennessine.
memoryHook: Berkelium sits below terbium, which is named for the village of Ytterby; Bk is likewise named for a place, Berkeley in California.

name: Californium
discoveredBy: Stanley Thompson, Kenneth Street, Albert Ghiorso and Glenn T. Seaborg
tagline: A working neutron source in metal form
about: Californium is one of the few synthetic elements made in genuinely useful amounts. Californium-252 decays partly by spontaneous fission, releasing neutrons at a steady rate, so a source the size of a grain can scan materials or start up a reactor. Producing it takes months of irradiation in high-flux research reactors.
memoryHook: Californium sits below dysprosium, but its name needs no decoding: it was made at the University of California, hence Cf.

name: Einsteinium
discoveredBy: Albert Ghiorso and co-workers at Berkeley, Argonne and Los Alamos
tagline: Found in the ash of a thermonuclear test
about: Einsteinium was identified in 1952 in debris from the first hydrogen bomb test, where uranium nuclei captured many neutrons at once. Named for Albert Einstein, it is now made only in milligram amounts at best, in high-flux reactors. Its isotopes decay within weeks to months, so most of what is known comes from microgram experiments.
memoryHook: Es for Einstein: the element was named for him in 1955, the year he died, after turning up in bomb debris three years earlier.

name: Fermium
discoveredBy: Albert Ghiorso and co-workers at Berkeley
tagline: Where neutron capture runs out of road
about: Fermium is the heaviest element that can be built up by neutron capture; past it the nuclei split before they can absorb more. It was found in 1952 in debris from a thermonuclear test and named for Enrico Fermi. Only trace, invisible quantities have ever been produced, so its bulk properties are predicted rather than measured.
memoryHook: Fermium, element 100, honours Enrico Fermi, who led the first controlled chain reaction: a round number for a nuclear pioneer.
elementalForm: Fm — metal, never isolated in bulk

name: Mendelevium
discoveredBy: Albert Ghiorso, Glenn T. Seaborg, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin and Stanley Thompson
tagline: Made one atom at a time, named for the table itself
about: Mendelevium is a synthetic actinide first made by bombarding einsteinium with helium ions, yielding just seventeen atoms. Only trace quantities have ever been produced, so its chemistry is followed by tracer methods and most listed properties are predicted rather than measured. Its longest-lived isotope has a half-life near 51 days.
memoryHook: Md honours Dmitri Mendeleev, who built the periodic table that predicted missing elements before anyone found them.

name: Nobelium
discoveredBy: Georgy Flerov and colleagues at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Dubna
tagline: The actinide that prefers a lower charge
about: Nobelium is a synthetic element whose discovery was claimed by three laboratories before credit settled on the Dubna team. Only trace numbers of atoms have ever been made, and most of its properties are predicted rather than measured. Unusually for an actinide, its stable ion in solution carries a 2+ charge rather than 3+.
memoryHook: No is named for Alfred Nobel, the chemist behind dynamite and the prizes; the symbol conveniently reads like the word no.

name: Lawrencium
discoveredBy: Albert Ghiorso, Torbjorn Sikkeland, Almon Larsh and Robert Latimer
tagline: Last actinide, with an unexpected outer electron
about: Lawrencium closes the actinide series and breaks its pattern: its outermost electron sits in a 7p orbital rather than the expected 6d, an effect traced to relativistic behavior in very heavy atoms. It has only ever been produced atom by atom, so nearly every listed property is predicted rather than measured.
memoryHook: Lr honours Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron, the accelerator type behind the creation of heavy elements like this one.

name: Rutherfordium
discoveredBy: Albert Ghiorso and colleagues at Berkeley, with a competing Dubna claim
tagline: The first element past the actinides
about: Rutherfordium is the first transactinide, sitting below hafnium in group 4. Only a few hundred atoms have ever been made and they decay within seconds, so nearly every listed property is predicted rather than measured. Gas-phase experiments suggest it behaves broadly like hafnium, with some relativistic deviations.
memoryHook: Rf honours Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the atomic nucleus that all superheavy element research now depends on.

name: Dubnium
discoveredBy: Albert Ghiorso and colleagues at Berkeley, with a competing Dubna claim
tagline: Named for the laboratory that chased it
about: Dubnium sits below tantalum in group 5 and exists only as a handful of atoms made in heavy-ion collisions. Its isotopes decay in seconds or minutes, so chemists work with single atoms and most listed properties are predicted rather than measured. Observed behavior broadly matches group 5 expectations.
memoryHook: Db is named for Dubna, the Russian town whose accelerator laboratory raced Berkeley to make and claim this element.

name: Seaborgium
discoveredBy: Albert Ghiorso, Kenneth Hulet and colleagues at Berkeley
tagline: A group 6 metal made a few atoms at a time
about: Seaborgium lies below tungsten in group 6 and has only ever existed as single atoms with half-lives measured in seconds. Experiments forming volatile oxide compounds showed chemistry resembling molybdenum and tungsten, supporting its place in the table. Its physical properties remain predictions rather than measurements.
memoryHook: Sg honours Glenn Seaborg, who was still alive when the name was approved, the first living person to be so honoured.

name: Bohrium
discoveredBy: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Munzenberg and colleagues at GSI Darmstadt
tagline: A heavier cousin of rhenium, briefly glimpsed
about: Bohrium was created at GSI in Darmstadt by fusing bismuth with chromium nuclei. Only a small number of atoms have been observed, each lasting seconds at most, so its physical properties are predicted rather than measured. Chemical studies of its volatile oxychloride placed it convincingly in group 7 with rhenium.
memoryHook: Bh honours Niels Bohr, whose model of quantised electron energy levels underpins how we describe atomic structure.

name: Hassium
discoveredBy: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Munzenberg and colleagues at GSI Darmstadt
tagline: Group 8 metal calculated to be extremely dense
about: Hassium belongs to group 8 alongside iron, ruthenium and osmium. Only a few dozen atoms have been made, each decaying within seconds, so its properties are predicted rather than measured; calculations point to an unusually dense bulk metal. Experiments with hassium tetroxide showed chemistry much like osmium.
memoryHook: Hs comes from Hassia, the Latin name for the German state of Hesse, home of the GSI laboratory that first made it.

name: Meitnerium
discoveredBy: Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Munzenberg and colleagues at GSI Darmstadt
tagline: Identified in 1982 from a single atom
about: Meitnerium was identified in 1982 from just one atom detected at GSI Darmstadt, and only a few more have been made since. No chemical experiment has yet been performed on it, so its placement below iridium in group 9 rests on theory. Every listed property is predicted rather than measured.
memoryHook: Mt honours Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission and was passed over by the Nobel committee that credited her colleague.

name: Darmstadtium
discoveredBy: Sigurd Hofmann, Victor Ninov and colleagues at GSI Darmstadt
tagline: Platinum's distant relative, known only by decay
about: Darmstadtium was first made by fusing lead and nickel nuclei, and only a handful of atoms have ever been detected. Its longest-lived isotopes survive for seconds, far too briefly for bulk chemistry, so every listed property is predicted. Theory places it below platinum in group 10, as yet unconfirmed by experiment.
memoryHook: Ds is named after Darmstadt, the German city whose GSI accelerator laboratory produced six elements in the periodic table.

name: Roentgenium
discoveredBy: Sigurd Hofmann and colleagues at GSI Darmstadt
tagline: Named for the physicist behind the first X-ray image
about: Roentgenium is a synthetic element first made at Darmstadt in 1994 by fusing nickel and bismuth nuclei. Only a few dozen atoms have ever existed, and the longest-lived isotopes survive for seconds at most. Everything known about it, including its predicted metallic character, comes from theory rather than measurement.
memoryHook: Rg honours Wilhelm Roentgen, discoverer of X-rays; the element was made in 1994, almost a century after that discovery.

name: Copernicium
discoveredBy: Sigurd Hofmann and colleagues at GSI Darmstadt
tagline: A heavyweight that may not be a metal at all
about: Copernicium was created at Darmstadt in 1996 from zinc and lead nuclei, and only a handful of atoms have ever been detected. Relativistic effects on its electrons are predicted to make it unusually volatile, perhaps closer to a noble gas than to mercury. Its measured half-lives run to seconds at most.
memoryHook: Cn = Copernicus. Element 112 was named on the 537th anniversary of his birth, which is why an astronomer's name sits in the table.

name: Nihonium
discoveredBy: Kosuke Morita's team at RIKEN, Japan
tagline: Japan's element, confirmed from just three atoms
about: Nihonium was first produced at RIKEN in Japan in 2004 by bombarding bismuth with zinc, and the team confirmed just three atoms over nearly a decade of searching. The isotopes seen so far decay within seconds. Every chemical property attributed to it is predicted rather than measured.
memoryHook: Nh comes from Nihon, one of the Japanese names for Japan, and marks the first element named by a research team in Asia.

name: Flerovium
discoveredBy: Yuri Oganessian's team at JINR Dubna with Lawrence Livermore
tagline: A doorway to the predicted island of stability
about: Flerovium was first detected at Dubna in 1998 and sits near the predicted island of stability, a region where superheavy nuclei should last longer than their neighbours. Only a few dozen atoms have been made, each decaying within seconds. Its chemistry is predicted, though single-atom work hints at real volatility.
memoryHook: Fl honours Georgy Flerov, founder of the Dubna laboratory. Think Flerov, not fluorine, which uses the single letter F.

name: Moscovium
discoveredBy: JINR Dubna and Lawrence Livermore collaboration
tagline: Fleeting atoms named for a Russian region
about: Moscovium was made at Dubna in 2003 by firing calcium ions at an americium target, and only a few dozen atoms have been detected since. Its known isotopes decay in well under a second. Everything said about its chemistry, including the expected heavy-metal behavior, is prediction rather than measurement.
memoryHook: Mc stands for Moscow. Element 115 is named for the Moscow region, where the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research first made it.

name: Livermorium
discoveredBy: JINR Dubna and Lawrence Livermore collaboration
tagline: Carries the name of a Californian laboratory
about: Livermorium was first observed at Dubna in 2000 in a collaboration with the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, whose name it carries. Fewer than a hundred atoms have been made, each surviving only milliseconds. Its position below polonium suggests metallic behavior, though that remains a prediction.
memoryHook: Lv is short for Livermore, the California laboratory that helped make it. Keep it apart from Lr, lawrencium, named for Ernest Lawrence.

name: Tennessine
discoveredBy: JINR Dubna, Oak Ridge and Vanderbilt collaboration
tagline: A halogen by position, a semimetal in theory
about: Tennessine was created in 2010 by a Russian-American team using a berkelium target produced at Oak Ridge in Tennessee. Although it sits in the halogen column, calculations predict semimetal behavior rather than anything like iodine or bromine. Only a few atoms have been made, each lasting milliseconds.
memoryHook: Tennessine ends in -ine like fluorine and chlorine, and it is named for Tennessee, whose Oak Ridge lab supplied the berkelium target.

name: Oganesson
discoveredBy: Yuri Oganessian's team at JINR Dubna with Lawrence Livermore
tagline: The end of the table, and no ordinary noble gas
about: Oganesson closes the seventh row and is the heaviest element yet confirmed. Fewer than ten atoms have ever been detected, each decaying in under a millisecond. Despite sitting below radon, calculations predict that it would not behave like a typical noble gas, and all of its properties remain theoretical.
memoryHook: Og is named for Yuri Oganessian, one of only two people to have an element named after them while still alive; the other was Glenn Seaborg.
